title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident describes a deliberate attempt to manipulate the training data and citation behavior of AI language models by flooding the information environment with fabricated institutional content. A fictitious think tank with no legal standing produced an extraordinary volume of text in a very short time using a platform built specifically to optimize content for AI ingestion. The failure is not one of an AI system malfunctioning but of AI systems being used as a target: if models learn from or cite web content without verifying the institutional legitimacy of sources, they can be made to launder propaganda as neutral research. Catching this at the AI layer would have required systematic checks on source authenticity before content influenced model outputs, checks that are not established practice in current deployment.

The operation was disclosed through a Justice Department filing, which means the link between the content and its funder entered the public record through a legal reporting mechanism rather than through any detection by the AI platforms themselves. The scale, over half a million words in nine days, suggests the strategy depends on volume and speed outpacing any human editorial review. That kind of velocity is only achievable with automated content generation, placing this squarely in the category of AI-assisted influence operations directed at other AI systems.

What is not established is whether any major AI model demonstrably changed its outputs as a result of this content, or whether the campaign achieved the influence on chatbot recommendations that it sought.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by Israel, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to optimize content for artificial intelligence systems. The institute, which has no legal entity status or physical address, presented pro-Israel arguments on topics including Palestinian torture, Israeli war crimes, and famine in Gaza, framing them as neutral research with academic citations. The operation was filed with the U.S. Justice Department as material distributed for the Israeli government, revealing efforts to influence what chatbots like ChatGPT cite and recommend to users.

The campaign is part of a broader Israeli government initiative worth tens of millions of dollars, routed through European advertising firm Havas Media and American contractors, to shape artificial intelligence responses to favor Israel's position. This effort comes as Israel's approval among Americans has significantly declined, with recent polling showing only 36 percent of Americans support Israel and 60 percent view it unfavorably. Israeli officials have expressed frustration that despite substantial spending on such public diplomacy campaigns, public opinion has worsened rather than improved.
